---
type: video-summary
video_id: EeBgUCYhezc
title: "SSAC19: DeepQB Deep Learning with Player Tracking to Quantify Quarterback Decision Makin Performance"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Brian Burke (caption spelling of host introduction); Nick de Yancey (host, caption spelling)]
topics: [american-football, decision-making, sports-science]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Brian Burke presents DeepQB, a neural network applied to NFL Next Gen Stats tracking data, built to measure quarterback decision-making apart from teammates and opponents. It predicts which of five eligible receivers the passer will target, the expected yardage, and whether the pass is completed, incomplete or intercepted. He argues earlier uses of tracking data amounted to a "fancy radar gun" [02:08]. The model picks the right target about 60 percent of the time, and he uses the gap between expected and observed yards per attempt as a performance measure. A fourth, quarterback-specific variant did not work well. He calls the work a proof of concept [23:32].

## Key claims

- Quarterback performance is hard to project, which he attributes to the position being cognitive and decision-driven [00:33].
- His past as a Navy fighter pilot shaped his interest in decisions under time pressure; he says a pilot has about three seconds and a quarterback about two and a half [01:38].
- Earlier tracking-data applications were limited to maximum speed and total distance [02:08].
- DeepQB uses a feed-forward neural network, described as a fairly standard deep learning type, with the same architecture reused for four variants [04:12].
- The model predicts the targeted receiver correctly about 60 percent of the time, which he frames as triple a one-in-five chance baseline [07:48].
- Completion rate is higher when the passer throws to the model's recommended receiver than when he does not [08:50].
- Proximity of a defender alone does not tell whether a receiver is targeted; one example showed a covered receiver the model and quarterback both chose [11:23].
- Yards above expectation can be credited to the quarterback as isolated performance [12:23].
- Rookies appear low on production relative to expectation and highly predictable [14:05].
- Agreement with the model shows a slight negative correlation with production, which he did not expect and attributes to selection bias, not tested in the talk [14:38].
- Aggregated decision-making explained little of interception differences; he judged most of one high-interception passer's rate came from inaccurate throws rather than poor decisions [17:43].
- The quarterback-specific variant, built with transfer learning, did not work as hoped [19:51].
- He says the approach can be run in reverse, aggregating by receiving corps or secondary [20:52].

## Numbers and definitions

- More than 45,000 targeted passes; training, validation and test sets drawn from the 2016 through 2018 seasons, test set is 2018 through week 12 [04:43], [05:13].
- Tracking data supplies position, speed, direction, acceleration and orientation, available about 10 seconds after a play [05:44].
- Chance baseline for target selection: one in five, or 20 percent; model accuracy about 60 percent [07:48].
- Completion percentage 74 percent when the quarterback throws to the recommended receiver, 55 percent otherwise, a factor of 1.4 [08:50].
- Example target probabilities: 80 percent [09:50], 15 percent [10:21], 8 percent and 77 percent [10:52].
- Goff example: model-expected 7.8 yards per attempt, actual 9.9 on targeted passes, difference +2.1 [12:54].
- Average predicted completion probability 79 percent for actual completions, 56 percent for actual incompletions [15:40].
- Yards per attempt above expected: the talk reports it for the top five and bottom five 2018 quarterbacks [12:54].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Feed-forward neural network with four variants: receiver target probability, expected yards, outcome probability, and a quarterback-tailored version of the first [04:43].
- Feature vector arranged by five eligible receivers: absolute and relative positions, velocities, orientations, receiver type, the nearest two defenders, game state, down, distance, yard line, play action, a binary duress flag, and quarterback velocity at release [06:15], [06:46].
- Mirror-image augmentation of each play to teach symmetry; he notes handedness is a flaw [07:16].
- Expected yards computed two ways: whole play configuration, or assuming each receiver is the target [12:23].
- Transfer learning: train all layers on all quarterbacks, freeze base layers, retrain on one quarterback [18:50].

## Limits and open questions

- The speaker calls this a proof of concept built on choices made to get a result [23:32].
- Model agreement correlated slightly negatively with production; the selection-bias explanation is offered without a test [14:38].
- The quarterback-specific variant gave odd similarity results, with a best performer least similar to others; his explanation involves running back targets and is unverified [19:51].
- Not isolated from receivers or scheme [20:52]; no hands, height or vertical information [22:01].
- Class imbalance for interceptions was not corrected [24:36].
- Results are from one test period, and 60 percent accuracy is his own framing of what counts as good [07:48].

## Q&A

- Asked whether he had reviewed results with quarterbacks: answer is garbled in captions [22:01].
- Asked about receiver quality: largely captured through velocity and separation, but hands and height are not [22:01].
- Asked about snapshots versus progressions: model can assume release at any time after the snap to find open receivers a quarterback missed [23:02].
- Asked about linemen and pressure: he says the project was a proof of concept and later work adds alignments and passing lanes [24:02].
- Asked about class imbalance: he did not rebalance interceptions because of time [24:36].

title: "SSAC19: Analytics for the Front Office: Valuing Protections on NBA Draft Picks"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Benjamin Foster; Michael Bins (co-author, caption spelling); Jonah (host)]
topics: [basketball, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Benjamin Foster, a PhD student in environmental sciences and engineering, presents a method for valuing NBA draft picks that carry protections, conditions that let a trading team keep a pick if it falls in a protected range. He treats a protected pick like a financial option and prices it in basketball terms (five-year win shares), not money. The system simulates team standings, builds outcome distributions by pick position, runs a Monte Carlo simulation, and adjusts for market risk with the Wang transform. A worked example on one traded pick shows protections removing about half its value. The goal is to help teams choose protections.

## Key claims

- Draft picks are trade assets, and protections change the distribution of outcomes the receiving team gets [03:36].
- Millions of protection schemes are possible, so one base pick can have millions of trade values [04:07].
- The NBA trade market is illiquid, and protections can help teams assemble trades they otherwise could not [04:37], [05:07].
- Traded protections cluster at top five, top 10 and top 14, which the authors read as psychological anchors on round numbers [05:38], [06:08].
- Protected picks parallel financial options, where volatility of the underlying value matters [07:40].
- Risk preference differs by pick: the first pick is priced risk-seeking, and picks 25 and 30 risk-averse [14:48].
- In the worked example, protections removed about half the value of the base pick [16:20].
- The model's findings lined up with what the Suns general manager said at the time of the trade, per the speaker [16:51], [17:22].
- Applications named: reviewing past trades, private negotiation of protections, possibly spotting mispriced assets, and pricing other assets such as Bird rights [20:25], [20:56].

## Numbers and definitions

- Player value metric: win shares summed over a player's first five years [11:45].
- Team standings simulated 10,000 times for roughly 20 remaining games [09:40]; Monte Carlo simulation also run 10,000 times [11:14].
- Seven asset classes from K-means clustering of pick outcome distributions [14:18].
- One bar in the output: a 16.8 percent chance of a player producing between 17 and a half and 21 and a half win shares [11:45], [12:16].
- Priced values: 43.1 win shares per five years unprotected, 21.0 protected [15:49]. Implied annual 8.6 unprotected, compared to a named player's 2018 season [15:49].
- Protections subtracted about 51 percent of the base pick's value [16:20].
- A 78 percent chance the pick would be protected in the first year [16:51].
- Next-year outcome range for the fourth-worst team: first worst to 24th worst, median eight [17:22].
- Protected pick priced at 4.2 (annual win shares, as spoken), against 4.5 for the player received in the prior year [17:52]. Caption note: 4.2 matches 21.0 divided by five; the unit is not stated in the captions.
- Market price of risk (gamma) is the single Wang-transform assumption, read generally as the market's risk preference [13:47], [14:18].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Three principles: characterize volatility of the underlying asset, assess contractual conditions, account for market risk [08:40].
- Module one: Elo-based season simulation giving a probability distribution of finishing position [09:10].
- Module two: cumulative distributions of win shares by pick position from historical Basketball-Reference data, for first-round picks [10:42].
- Monte Carlo combining lottery probabilities and protection schemes [11:14].
- Wang transform, with market price of risk calibrated on pick-for-pick trades and interpolated where needed [13:17], [14:48].

## Limits and open questions

- Calibration of risk parameters rests on few pick-for-pick trades; the speaker says more work is needed [14:48].
- Simulation does not account for player movement, and the work was done on personal computers with limited time [19:23].
- The example comparison omits team-building considerations such as an expiring contract [18:22].
- Time discounting and option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled [22:26].
- Win shares was chosen for simplicity; other metrics could be swapped in [10:11].
- The explanation for round-number clustering is a hypothesis [06:08].

## Q&A

- Asked about discounting for player performance and the future option value of rolling over picks: the speaker said time considerations are hard to frame in a market sense and are not explicitly handled [22:26].
